title: The child at the well
hook: Mencius: anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm, and that is the seed of goodness (Mencius 2A.6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Good Samaritan stopped on the Jericho road. Your line was go and do likewise. Who did you stop for? Day seventy-eight.

A new week, and a week of many houses: China, India, the Sikh Gurus, the Gospels and the Buddha, one story from each, each kept by its own people. We begin with an old argument. Are people basically good? Or basically selfish, and just good at hiding it? The news on a bad day will give you one answer. A stranger carrying your groceries will give you the other. A Chinese philosopher named Mencius answered with a picture you can see in an instant. Today's story is the child at the well.
screen: `A WEEK OF MANY HOUSES.` → `ARE PEOPLE BASICALLY GOOD?` → `A PICTURE YOU SEE IN AN INSTANT.`

segments.voice: Mencius was a teacher in the line of Confucius, and later tradition called him the second sage, honored next to Confucius himself. The book of his teachings is simply called the Mencius. In one passage, he says every person has a heart that can't bear to see others suffer. And here's his proof. Suppose someone suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he says, would feel a jolt of alarm and distress. And then he rules out the other explanations one by one. It isn't because you want to get in good with the child's parents. It isn't because you want your neighbors and friends to praise you. It isn't because you'd dislike what people would say, or, as some read the line, the sound of the child crying. It's there before any of that. It's just there. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say everyone runs and saves the child. The picture stops at the jolt, the first flash, before any decision. That flash, Mencius says, is a sprout. He names four of them: the heart of compassion, the heart of shame, the heart of courtesy, and the heart that knows right from wrong. Everyone has them, like having four limbs. But sprouts have to be grown, like a small fire catching or a spring starting to flow. Not every Confucian agreed. A later thinker named Xunzi argued the opposite: that goodness has to be trained into people from the outside. Chinese tradition kept both voices. And Mencius's picture stays simple. In his telling, a flinch at someone else's pain isn't weakness, and it isn't for show. It's the seed.
screen: `MENCIUS, IN THE LINE OF CONFUCIUS.` · `A CHILD ABOUT TO FALL.` · `NOT FOR PRAISE, NOT FOR THANKS.` · `FOUR SPROUTS, TO BE GROWN.` · then, large: `THE SEED IS THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your first kind impulse today. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Was there a moment when something in you leaned toward someone else: a wince when a friend was hurt, a wish to help a stranger, a flash of care before you thought about it? Find one. Don't judge whether you acted on it. Just notice that it was there, before any reasons arrived. That's one of Mencius's sprouts. Let your attention rest on it, like sun on a seedling. The bell holds the time.
The child at the well. Mencius's picture of the jolt anyone feels, before any reason, and the sprout of goodness inside it. Today's word.
screen: `THE CHILD AT THE WELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the seed is there. Today, when you feel that first small pull toward someone, notice it, and give it a little water. Day seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Students of Confucian thought learn the child at the well as Mencius's case that human nature is good, and read it alongside Xunzi's opposite view.

fork.setup: you're Mencius, asked to prove people have a heart for others. what do you offer?
options: a child about to fall into a well
fork.reveal: a child about to fall into a well. anyone would feel alarm, he says, not for praise or favor, and that jolt is the sprout of goodness.

original.note: Chinese, ceyin zhi xin: the heart of compassion, the first of Mencius's four sprouts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a philosopher saying everyone is nice.
what it means: the first jolt of care is there in everyone, a sprout that still has to be grown.
what a scholar hears: Mencius 2A.6, the four sprouts (duan), and the long debate with Xunzi over human nature.

notes: Mencius 2A.6 paraphrased (Legge's 1861 translation is public domain, but the wording was not certain enough to quote). Confirm the three ruled-out motives and the four sprouts: compassion, shame, courtesy/deference, right and wrong.
Mencius dates (c. 372–289 BCE by tradition): the script says 'the three hundreds BCE'.
Chinese 惻隱之心 (ceyin zhi xin) and the rough pronunciation: confirm.
Xunzi presented neutrally as a dissenting Confucian voice.

Reviewer edit: the third ruled-out motive (惡其聲) is read two ways: Legge and Zhu Xi take 聲 as reputation (dislike of being known as unmoved), some modern translators as the sound of the child's cries. Script now gives both; confirm.
Reviewer edit: 'the most honored thinker after Confucius' softened to the traditional title 'second sage' (亞聖): confirm.

Editor review (days 76-94 pass): cut the unsourced dates (twenty-three centuries ago, the three hundreds BCE) and the 'two seconds' count; the closing line no longer tells the listener what they feel; howItsDone no longer claims memorization 'for many centuries'.
